title: Episode 187: Gerald R. Ford: The Accidental President, the Pardon, and Chevy Chase (1974–1977)
description:
Gerald Rudolph Ford Jr. was the only chief executive in American history who became both Vice President and President without winning a single national election. A star center on the University of Michigan's undefeated national championship football teams and a decorated World War II combat naval officer, Ford was universally beloved on Capitol Hill for his absolute honesty, modesty, and lack of pretense. Sworn into the presidency upon Richard Nixon's resignation, Ford disarmed the nation with his humble inaugural declaration: 'I am a Ford, not a Lincoln.' Just one month later, Ford stunned the world by granting Nixon a full and unconditional pardon, sacrificing his own political future to close the wounds of Watergate. Enduring two assassination attempts in seventeen days and laughing off Chevy Chase's weekly physical parodies on the debut season of Saturday Night Live, Ford restored trust, decency, and calm to a fractured republic. Discover the warmth and integrity of America's thirty-eighth president.

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the good-humored, decent world of Gerald R. Ford. Thrust into the presidency during the darkest constitutional crisis of the twentieth century, Ford brought honesty, warmth, and unpretentious Midwestern decency to a traumatized White House. Here is George with the story of the accidental president, the controversial pardon, and the healing of the nation.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE ALL-AMERICAN CENTER FROM GRAND RAPIDS
Gerald Rudolph Ford Jr. was born Leslie Lynch King Jr. in Omaha, Nebraska, in July 1913. When his abusive biological father threatened his mother with a knife just sixteen days after his birth, his mother fled with her infant to Grand Rapids, Michigan. There, she married Gerald R. Ford Sr., a hardworking paint and varnish salesman who formally adopted the boy, raising him with strict Christian values, personal modesty, and hard work. Young 'Jerry' was an extraordinary natural athlete. Enrolling at the University of Michigan, Ford played center and linebacker, leading the Wolverines to consecutive undefeated national championships in 1932 and 1933 and earning team Most Valuable Player honors. He turned down lucrative professional contract offers from both the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions, choosing instead to coach boxing and football at Yale while earning his law degree. During World War II, Lieutenant Ford served as assistant navigator aboard the light aircraft carrier USS Monterey in the Pacific, earning ten battle stars and narrowly surviving the terrifying December 1944 Typhoon Cobra, during which he was nearly swept off the rolling flight deck into the churning ocean. Returning home to Grand Rapids, Ford was elected to Congress in 1948, beginning a quarter-century of honest, unblemished service in the House of Representatives. Ford's athletic discipline and courage under fire in the Pacific forged in him an unshakeable inner calm, modesty, and personal integrity that guided his every decision. His Midwestern roots and collegiate athletic honors instilled in Ford a genuine modesty that never abandoned him, even in the Oval Office.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE 25TH AMENDMENT MIRACLE
For eight years as House Minority Leader, Ford was the most trusted and respected Republican in Washington, renowned for his warm bipartisan friendships with Democratic leaders like Tip O'Neill. In October 1973, in the midst of the Watergate firestorm, Vice President Spiro Agnew resigned in disgrace after pleading no contest to federal tax evasion and accepting cash bribes in his office. Under the newly ratified Twenty-Fifth Amendment, President Nixon was required to nominate a successor subject to confirmation by both houses of Congress. Congressional leaders informed Nixon that Gerald Ford was the only Republican whom both Democrats and Republicans would confirm without a bitter partisan fight. Confirmed overwhelmingly by votes of ninety-two to three in the Senate and three hundred and eighty-seven to thirty-five in the House, Ford took the oath as Vice President in December 1973. Eight short months later, when Nixon resigned, Gerald Ford was catapulted into the presidency—the only man in American history to reach the highest office without ever being elected on a national presidential or vice presidential ticket. His confirmation as Vice President by overwhelming bipartisan majorities demonstrated the universal respect he commanded across both sides of the congressional aisle. His appointment demonstrated the genius of the Twenty-Fifth Amendment, allowing the republic to execute a seamless transition of power in the midst of scandal.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: 'A FORD, NOT A LINCOLN': AUGUST 9, 1974
At twelve-five in the afternoon on August 9, 1974, Gerald R. Ford took the oath of office in the East Room of the White House before a somber, exhausted gathering of government leaders and his vibrant wife, Betty Ford. In an era poisoned by executive secrecy, imperial pretensions, and cynicism, Ford delivered an inaugural address that was disarmingly simple, honest, and humble. 'I am acutely aware,' he began, 'that you have not elected me as your President by your ballots, and so I ask you to confirm me as your President with your prayers... I have not sought this enormous responsibility, but I will not shirk it.' Then came his famous, folksy contrast with his illustrious predecessors: 'I am a Ford, not a Lincoln. My fellow Americans, our long national nightmare is over. Our Constitution works; our great Republic is a government of laws and not of men. Here the people rule.' Ford announced an open-door policy with the press, insisted on making his own English muffins in the morning toaster, and brought an immediate, refreshing breath of fresh air into the executive mansion. That moving declaration that 'our long national nightmare is over' lifted a suffocating weight of cynicism from the American consciousness, ushering in a new era of executive transparency. Ford's unpretentious personal style, preparing his own breakfast and welcoming journalists with warmth, helped dissolve the toxic atmosphere left by Watergate.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE GREAT NIXON PARDON SHOCKWAVE
Ford's political honeymoon lasted exactly one month. As federal prosecutors prepared criminal indictments against Richard Nixon, Ford realized that a prolonged criminal trial of a former president would consume Washington for years, inflaming partisan hatreds, paralyzing the judicial system, and dominating every single day of his own administration. Concluding that his paramount duty was to heal the nation's wounds, Ford made a agonizing, solitary decision. On Sunday morning, September 8, 1974, speaking to the nation from the Oval Office, Ford announced that he was granting Richard Nixon 'a full, free, and absolute pardon... for all offenses against the United States' committed during his presidency. The public reaction was an explosion of volcanic fury: critics accused Ford of striking a corrupt 'secret deal' to secure the presidency, his press secretary Jerald terHorst resigned in protest, and Ford's public approval rating plummeted overnight from seventy-one percent to forty-nine percent. Yet decades later, historical consensus completely vindicated Ford. In 2001, Senator Edward Kennedy presented Gerald Ford with the prestigious John F. Kennedy Profile in Courage Award, admitting that while he had fiercely opposed the pardon in 1974, time had proven it to be one of the most selfless, noble acts of statesmanship in presidential history. The controversial pardon of Richard Nixon sacrificed Ford's own political standing for the sake of the country's long-term healing, an enduring act of selfless moral leadership. In choosing national reconciliation over personal popularity, Ford accepted the political cost of the pardon with quiet, selfless dignity.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE KLUTZ MYTH AND THE CHEVY CHASE SPOOF
Despite being one of the most coordinated, athletic presidents in American history, Ford became the victim of a comical media trope: the clumsy, bumbling klutz. The myth began in June 1975, when Ford slipped on a wet ramp while disembarking from Air Force One in the pouring rain in Salzburg, Austria. Television cameras captured the brief stumble, airing it repeatedly. In October 1975, a revolutionary new late-night comedy show debuted on NBC called Saturday Night Live. Young comedian Chevy Chase made Ford his signature impression, opening Weekend Update by stumbling through podiums, tangling himself in telephone cords, dropping glasses, and tumbling over furniture. Rather than taking offense or retaliating, Ford displayed his characteristic, generous good humor. In April 1976, Ford invited Chevy Chase to perform beside him at the White House Radio and Television Correspondents' Dinner. After Chase accidentally knocked over his water glass and podium, President Ford stood up, gave a deadpan speech, and deliberately pulled a napkin out of his suit pocket, causing a shower of silverware to clatter onto the floor, bringing down the house with laughter and turning the joke on himself. His genuine, self-deprecating good humor in the face of comedic satire disarmed the press and endeared him to millions of Americans who recognized his decency. His willingness to participate in the humor alongside Chevy Chase showed a leader who possessed the rare wisdom not to take himself too seriously.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: TWO ASSASSINATION ATTEMPTS IN SEVENTEEN DAYS
Behind the laughter, Ford faced genuine, terrifying mortal danger. In September 1975, while traveling in California, Ford survived two separate assassination attempts in seventeen days—both carried out by women. On September 5, in Sacramento, twenty-six-year-old Lynette 'Squeaky' Fromme, a fanatical disciple of mass murderer Charles Manson, drew a loaded .45 caliber semi-automatic pistol from a leg holster and pointed it point-blank at Ford's chest from two feet away as he shook hands in a crowd. Secret Service agent Larry Buendorf lunged, wedging his hand into the pistol's slide mechanism to prevent the hammer from striking the cartridge, tackling Fromme to the ground. Seventeen days later, on September 22 in San Francisco, forty-five-year-old political radical Sara Jane Moore stood in a crowd outside the St. Francis Hotel and fired a shot from a .38 caliber revolver at Ford as he walked to his limousine. An alert disabled Marine veteran standing beside her, Oliver Sipple, grabbed her arm as she squeezed the trigger, deflecting the bullet into the pavement and saving the President's life. Ford displayed remarkable composure, calmly walking to his car and continuing his public duties. Ford's unflinching courage in the face of two assassination attempts in California revealed a steady, stoic fatalism and an absolute devotion to his public duties. In surviving two assassination attempts with total composure, Ford demonstrated the physical and moral courage of a decorated wartime veteran.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE BICENTENNIAL SUMMER AND HEALING THE REPUBLIC
The crowning moment of Gerald Ford's presidency arrived in the glorious summer of 1976: the United States Bicentennial. On the Fourth of July, 1976, President Ford presided over the magnificent parade of 'Tall Ships' from thirty nations sailing up the Hudson River into New York Harbor. Speaking at Valley Forge and the Liberty Bell in Philadelphia, Ford captured the joyful, revived spirit of a country that had survived depression, world war, political assassination, and constitutional crisis: 'We can be very proud of what we have done, and we can be very confident of what we will do.' In the election of 1976, running against Democratic outsider Jimmy Carter, Ford staged a remarkable late-campaign surge, closing a thirty-point polling deficit to lose by a razor-thin margin of two percentage points. When Jimmy Carter took the oath of office in January 1977, Carter's very first inaugural words were a moving tribute: 'For myself and for our nation, I want to thank my predecessor for all he has done to heal our land.' Gerald Ford had assumed the presidency of a broken nation, restored decency and dignity to the White House, and left the American republic whole again. The joyful celebration of the 1976 Bicentennial stood as a triumphant testament to the healing of the nation, restoring pride and confidence to the American spirit. The Bicentennial of 1976 provided the joyful emotional closure that allowed the nation to turn the page on a turbulent decade.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Gerald R. Ford healed a fractured nation with unpretentious Midwestern honesty and boundless good humor. To succeed him, the American people turned to a devout, soft-spoken peanut farmer from Georgia who promised never to tell a lie: James Earl Carter Jr. Next week, we begin our exploration of Jimmy Carter: his training under Admiral Hyman Rickover, his heroism during a nuclear reactor meltdown in Canada, his historic walk down Pennsylvania Avenue, and the triumph of the Camp David Accords. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
